# Migrations

Migrations are Go files in the program's `migrations` package, each
registering its operations from `init`. The schema a database has is the
replay of its migrations; `makemigrations` compares the replay with the
models the program declares and writes the difference as the next file.
Django's model, with Go files you review and edit.

```go
// migrations/0001_initial.go — generated by orm makemigrations.
package migrations

import m "github.com/vuka-lang/orm/migration"

func init() {
	m.Register(m.Migration{
		Name: "0001_initial",
		Operations: []m.Operation{
			m.CreateModel{
				Table: "users",
				Fields: []m.NamedField{
					m.F("id", m.BigAuto()),
					m.F("name", m.Varchar(100).Unique()),
					m.F("email", m.Varchar(200)),
				},
			},
		},
	})
}
```

The program imports the package, so `orm.Migrate` (and the commands) see
the migrations:

```vuka
import _ "example.com/blog/migrations"

func run(ctx context.Context) error {
	db := orm.ConnectURL(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))?
	orm.AddDatabase("main", db, orm.AsDefault())
	return orm.Migrate(ctx)                // pending migrations, under a lock
}
```

## The orm command

```sh
go run github.com/vuka-lang/orm/cmd/orm makemigrations [name]
go get -tool github.com/vuka-lang/orm/cmd/orm    # then: go tool orm …
```

| Command | |
|---|---|
| `orm makemigrations [name]` | write the next migration from the models' changes |
| `orm migrate [target\|zero]` | apply every database's pending migrations, or take one database to `target`, unapplying later ones (`zero`: all) |
| `orm showmigrations` | `[X]`/`[ ]` per migration, per database |
| `orm sqlmigrate <name>` | a migration's SQL for the database's dialect |
| `orm generate [dir]` | write `orm_scanners_gen.go`: the models' registrations and reflection-free row scanners |

| Flag | |
|---|---|
| `--db name` | the database (makemigrations, migrate, sqlmigrate); the default otherwise |
| `--check` | fail when a migration (or a generated file) is missing, writing nothing: for CI |
| `--dry-run` | print the migration instead of writing it |
| `--empty` | a migration with an empty `RunGo`, for a data migration |
| `--noinput` | ask nothing: a rename is written as a removal and an addition |
| `--backwards` | sqlmigrate: the SQL unapplying it |
| `--dialect` | `postgres`, `mysql` (`mysql/9.3.0` for a server version), `sqlite`: the SQL of another dialect |
| `--database name=URL` | a database's URL (repeatable; `default=` for the default); else `DATABASE_URL` and `DATABASE_URL_<NAME>` |
| `--default name` | the default database's name, as the models name it |
| `--main dir` | the program's main package, when the module has several |

On a terminal `makemigrations` asks about renames — "Did you rename
users.mail to users.email? [y/N]".

The commands build the program's main package with an init overlaid that
answers them before `main` runs; nothing is written to the tree but the
migration file. The program links the drivers it opens.

## Vuka models

A module with `.vuka` files is built through `vuka gen` (the `vuka` command on
the `PATH`, or `VUKA`), and the tool's init runs after the main package's own,
so its models' field attributes and registrations are in. Nothing else
changes: `orm makemigrations` in a Vuka project reads `@orm.Char{Max: 200}`
as it would read a tag.

`orm generate` is optional — without it rows are read by reflection — and in
a Vuka project `@orm.Entity` registers a model without it.

## Operations

| Operation | |
|---|---|
| `m.CreateModel{Table, Fields, Indexes}`, `m.DeleteModel`, `m.RenameModel` | tables |
| `m.AddField`, `m.RemoveField`, `m.AlterField`, `m.RenameField` | columns |
| `m.AddIndex`, `m.RemoveIndex`, `m.AddConstraint`, `m.RemoveConstraint` | indexes, constraints |
| `m.CreateExtension{Name}` | a Postgres extension (`vector`, `pg_trgm`) |
| `m.CreateFunction{…}` | an SQL [function](/orm/expressions#sql-functions-in-a-migration) |
| `m.RunSQL`, `m.RunGo` | anything else; a data migration |

Fields are written with builders — `m.BigAuto()`, `m.Varchar(n)`, `m.Text()`,
`m.BigInt().FK("users", "id").OnDelete(m.Cascade)`, `m.Time().Null().Index()`,
`m.Vector(3)` — and per-dialect SQL with `m.Dialects{Postgres, MySQL,
SQLite}`. `orm.CreateExtension("vector")` declares an extension for the next
migration from the program.

## At run time

`orm.Migrate(ctx, opts…)` applies pending migrations under a lock (a Postgres
advisory lock, MySQL's `GET_LOCK`), recording them in `orm_migrations`
(`orm.MigrationsTable`; a program coming from nexus sets
`nexus_migrations`):

| | |
|---|---|
| `orm.MigrateOn("main")` | one database |
| `orm.MigrateLogger(l)` | log what is applied |
| `orm.ApplyMigrations(ctx, db, target, migs…)` | a given list (tools, tests) |
| `orm.Schema{}.Verify(ctx, models…)` | check the models against a database (a schema of it) at start-up |

In a web app, [`ormweb`](/orm/databases#web-integration)'s
`.MigrateOnStart(true)` runs them as the databases open.

## Several databases

Each database has its own migrations: the default's in `migrations/`, another
database's in `migrations/<db>/` (its own package, imported too). A model's
table is migrated on the database its writes go to, and on its `Mirror`:

```sh
orm makemigrations --db analytics    # migrations/analytics/ with the models routed there
orm migrate                          # every database's
orm migrate --db analytics 0003_sales
```

Routers registered at init (for the command, which runs before `main`) route
the tables, and every router's `AllowMigrate` must allow it. See
[Multiple databases](/orm/databases#multiple-databases).
